title: Notes of Ministry - 64 - March 1978

paragraphs.text: The title “man of God” is specially used of these two great prophets, Elijah and Elisha, and I have little doubt that in using the same expression to Timothy Paul must have had these prophets in his mind. It is not, it seems, an expression specially denoting gift, though these men would be in the fullest sense prophets, but it does seem to bring in that the man is expressive in some sense of the power of God. It is a concern at this present time that there be power to promote life among the brethren. The suggestion is not that life is wanting; the suggestion is the positive one of the need to maintain what is in life and in freshness constantly for the pleasure of God. What I am, and what every person is, in the local assembly will carry an influence of one kind or another. The point is that that influence should be positive and stimulating to life among the brethren. We see how, in addressing himself to Timothy, the beloved apostle has in mind, more particularly perhaps in his second letter, to rekindle the features of life. How effectively he did it! These two epistles have come to us peculiarly in times of recovery, tending to strengthen what is in life; and that is the concern as to this occasion.

We must have noticed how these two prophets, Elijah and Elisha, both had to do with a dead child. The same concern as to a dead child is faced by both; Elijah, I suppose, presents to us in some sense the glory of a man going into heaven, relating to the glory of Christ; Elisha asserts what belongs in our time to the Holy Spirit. Both prophets bring power to bear, and the manner of their doing so is remarkable as to its detail; they were able to bring what was in death to life. The point in mind in speaking of this is to see what will constantly tend to bring in life among the people of God. We may not be faced with the extreme case of moral death; thank God if our dear young ones, especially, are sustained in life; but we are to maintain the spirit of life and freshness in persons by our influence and activity.

The circumstances are very affecting in both cases. The maternal side is so much affected in both, and we need that maternal side of things among us. We need the element that will care for what is living and will seek to nourish it. We need all the feeling features of watchful, tender care that constitute the mother. In the first instance it says, as the matter is concluded, that Elijah delivered the child to his mother. He recognises the force and necessity of the mother, as if to place the child in the mother’s particular responsibility. It is as if the prophet would say, ‘What I have needed to do, I have done. Now this child, brought from death, is in your care’. And that is something, I believe, for us to take to heart. The maternal side of things involves in our time the sisterhood, but not only the sisterhood; it is the side of care in the assembly in which all would have part, watchful for the features of life to appear, and moving in a way that would strengthen every element of life in every person in the company. It is a very attractive thought in the working of it in our several localities.

We have before us, in this first passage especially, the feeling side of matters, “Let this child’s soul come into him again”; it is a feature of life in which God delights that there is what is of soul in persons, involving depth in the affections and feelings. When this prophet is presented to us he has his “upper chamber where he abode”. I point to that briefly as a most needed element with us in working out the concern for life in local meetings. Do I know what it is to be in secret with God? Have I an upper chamber? I would say affectionately from this scripture to every brother and sister. Have you an upper chamber? Do you know what it is to withdraw from every other kind of influence, get into the presence of God, and find strength and power there? The upper chamber is a prime necessity of a man of God. We well know that the demands of these times leave us in our personal and household circumstances very little time to get quietly and restfully into God’s presence, but we need to make time for that.

There may be the need to sacrifice less necessary things. There may be the need for greater definiteness, that we are not found wanting in the use of the upper chamber. There we learn God, and God is graciously pleased to make communications to us and leave us with impressions that sustain us in life. I am not speaking now, I need scarcely say, of life eternal, as we had it in the reading, but of the more general sense of life in that what is living is maintained among the people of God.

How God delights in life! He brought in the elements of it in creation and set them in their place, and then He brought man in and breathed into him the breath of life, giving to man a moral being unique and distinct from all the creatures that had been created. That whole scene, as has often been said, was teeming with life. And the assembly, secured for God’s pleasure, is to be like that, teeming with life. There will be those who are more mature, who have been long in the pathway, anticipating that the Lord may soon take them. Then there are the younger ones, and there are all the stages of growth in between; the little children, the young men, and the fathers are all represented, but life, what is fresh, is to mark them all. There are persons we know, and have known, like this. We are thankful to reflect that we know them now, those who always tend to life. If we become engaged in conversation with such their conversation relates to what is living, and it tends to infect you with what is living, which is a great positive end in mind. If we speak of the things of life we tend to disseminate the things of life among the brethren. If we speak of the things of death we shall not help on the living quality of things very much, as I need scarcely say.

Here was a man, a prophet, who had his upper chamber, and he carried the child to his upper chamber. He went before God alone as to this child. He found in that the power he needed to bring in healing. He stretched himself upon the child three times. There is no question, I think, that those three times refer to death and resurrection, the dying and resurrection of Jesus; there is the bringing to bear upon this child of the full powerful efficacy of the death of Christ and His glorious resurrection. Can we bring what is in Christ to bear upon one another, so that what relates to death may be met, and what relates to life introduced? He stretched himself three times. That is, it was not without exercise, it was no mere mechanical movement; it calls for a certain nearness in the application of the truth. So let us keep near to one another; let no estrangement come

in, however small. Let not little things be magnified into estrangements. I have nothing specific in mind in saying that, save the tendency sometimes for it to happen. But the spirit of Elijah the prophet, asserting what is related to the glory of Christ, would rise above all these small things and just come into nearness to the child. It is a most challenging thing, but can we do it? Can we get near enough to a person to stimulate the elements of life there? It is a choice matter, delightful to God.

What comes to light is a son—“See, thy son lives”. What a wonderful evidence of God’s hand in blessing, not only a son, but a son in life! We would love to see all the brethren bearing this character, sonship in life, sustaining not only the right to have a place in the realm of sonship, but sustaining in life the realities of what belongs to sonship in the presence of God—a fine objective! God would have us make it our objective, that we might come out in this character of the man of God, able to bring what is of God to bear upon persons and strengthen and enliven and help them. The bonds that unite us are very close in these days; we thank God that is so. The little estrangements that I have spoken of, in general, thank God, are notably absent. But let us watch that the enemy does not get in at any place, at any time, to bring about any barrier against this choice activity of strengthening and stimulation that tends to life in all the brethren; let us be set for it in a definite way.

Then we come to Elisha, in principle bringing us to the Spirit’s day. It says of him that “He went up, and lay upon the child, and put his mouth upon his mouth, and his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands”. You might wonder why so much detail is given; it is to bring out that the prophet is bringing something to bear upon the child of a distinctive kind. He lay upon the child, and put his mouth upon his mouth. How would Elisha speak? How would this child speak? It is intended, I believe, to show here that Elisha is imparting something to the child that relates to what he stands for in himself. Before we can do this we have to stand for something ourselves. The need is that we have qualities in ourselves, and how blessed it is that we have the Spirit on whom to rely to bring out features at any time when they are specially needed. Do we know the Spirit well enough? Are our links with the Spirit strong enough? Is our reference to the Spirit frequent enough? Are we kept, in the course of our walk in our pathways here, close enough to Him who is “another Comforter” according to the words of Jesus? Is there not yet scope for us to be kept in greater practical nearness to the Spirit of God? I have to say that is what I feel for myself. Elisha, I believe, illustrates it. He has got something. The mouth of Elisha means something. He is concerned to bring what corresponds with it into this child. He is, so to say, seizing features that are pleasing to God and seeking to inculcate those features in life into the child.

Then there were his eyes. Elisha must have had remarkable vision. His prophetic actings and speakings suggest a remarkable view of what God was doing. He would give some range of that vision to this young person. And then it says, “his hands upon his hands”. What would the hands of Elisha do? What would Elisha put his hands to? No mere trivialities or unimportant things; coming forth from God, as he did, the man of God, he would put his hand to weighty matters, and he would provoke the same thing in life in this child. So what is
according to God in the man of God is disseminated, it expands in the circle of the brethren, it expands in the fellowship. But then, are we possessed of such qualities, beloved brethren?

The work of God, is going on rapidly in these days; we marvel at the skill of it. I believe there is to be yet more striving that we take on the features of the heavenly Man, features that the Spirit would promote. We are to find grace in our contacts one with another to strengthen those features in our brethren as having some degree of possession of them in ourselves. In this sense the assembly becomes a living order of things practically in the personal relationships that enter into it; life is thus disseminated in all its characteristics and features among the brethren, and that, I believe, is very pleasing to God.

It says later that “He returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and bent over him”. Twice it says of Elisha that he bent over him. Can we bend, dear brethren? Can we take a low place? Is the spirit of Christ in humility characteristically marking us? It tends always to resolve every difficulty when the spirit of Christ in humility is at work. We long to be able to bring it in; we long to see it coming into expression. We thank God that it does come into expression; in this time of the Spirit, the spirit of Jesus, in that sense the spirit of the lowly Man, is being brought out in the saints. It is a prime feature in the Spirit’s day. The Spirit Himself, blessed be His Person, has taken a place so lowly in the saints, and He would have us to take on this feature of lowliness, the feature which Paul had in mind when he said to the Philippian brethren, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus”, Philippians 2: 5.

There are references in Scripture, such as that to Abigail, that show us the bearing of going down. What lowliness of spirit we see in Hannah, too, in her song! It is as if we are to be reminded that such a spirit as this is what God looks for in persons in the assembly in these times of the Spirit. Let us find the capacity, as having Christ in our hearts and the spirit of Christ before us, to bend, dear brethren. The prophet bent over the child twice. Can we do that? Can we get down to the situation, as humbly taking the ground that Elisha takes in this passage, to bring some effect in from God that shall result in life? One longs for it, that there may be not only the bringing in, but the sustaining in life, as we take humble ground and accustom ourselves to this concern to go down, to bend in the presence of that in which help is needed.

Well, with this background, we have Paul saying to Timothy, “But thou, O man of God, flee these things”. One senses sometimes that it would perhaps have been something of a surprise to Timothy when he found himself being addressed as a man of God. It would arouse concern with him that he might genuinely fill out that place in a substantial sense. I believe it was a skilful touch on Paul’s part, to awaken Timothy to a full sense of the responsibility that lay upon him. Timothy was a young man, as we are given to understand. He is not one of those more mature persons, in years at least. He was a young man, and yet the beloved apostle addresses him in this way, as if he would bring out the full features of the man of God in Timothy. So Paul goes on to intimate the features that are needed, “righteousness, piety, faith, love, endurance, meekness of spirit. Strive earnestly in the good conflict of faith. Lay hold of eternal life, to which thou hast been called, and hast confessed the good confession before many

witnesses”. These are the features of life, the features that prove the quality of what life is in men, as brought out in the man of God. There is to be some reflection of this, I verily believe, in these closing moments among those who love Christ and know the Spirit and who delight in what is due to God; there is to be capacity to affect situations so that life is introduced, and life is sustained. Through that the pleasure of God shall be maintained until the Lord comes.
May God bless the word.

I refer to these scriptures, beloved brethren, in order to promote exercise and, I trust, accord among us in relation to the question. Is there continuity in the recovery or is there not? One might think as seeking to hold the ground that there is such continuity, that the question was not of prime importance nor need it be significantly considered. But the question is raised. It comes up in readings from time to time; it comes up, also, in other ways, and while the saints are not to be troubled “by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2: 2), it is well if questions that do arise are worked out in exercise in our spirits, so that we can ourselves each intelligently and committedly give the answer to them.

The question is really whether, ever since the Lord began His great work in recovery one hundred and fifty years ago, there has been a continuous line down to the present day which we may expect to continue to the rapture, or has the incidence of various things in history interrupted that line? and if we believe that, that that line has been interrupted, then we must also admit that at some point, if there is anything here for the Lord, He must have had to begin again. I think that that conclusion is inescapable and that if the matter is presented in that way, the affirmation that there has been continuity will ring in the minds of the brethren.

I refer to these two scriptures in Corinthians because it will be noticed, as has often been noticed before, that the address to the assembly in Corinth is the same in both epistles, “the assembly of God which is in Corinth”. While different matters come into the opening of Paul’s addresses to this assembly, the greeting is the same, “Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ”. The address and the greeting are the same and you might therefore conclude that in Paul’s mind there was continuity in Corinth. You might, however, say—and some who raise contention about these things say things like this—‘But there was sin in Corinth, there was failure there, there was breakdown there, there was unjudged evil there’, and the simplest reader of the first epistle will realise that those things are all true. Not to condone them, but the things that were actually gone on with in Corinth are in our day amazing. Doctrinally things were amazing—there were brethren breaking bread who did not believe in the resurrection. “How say some among you that there is not a resurrection of those that are dead?”, 1 Corinthians 15: 12. There were some who came to the Supper and took their own meal before others and, indeed, put to shame others of their brethren, and that in a local assembly. And Paul has to say to them, “When ye come therefore together … it is not to eat the Lord’s supper”, 1 Corinthians 11: 20. That is to say, some other objective was before them, or alternatively, that what they took in the shape of the Supper could not rightly be dignified by that name. And there were divisions among them which were evidently publicly known and there was sin among them which was outrageous, even in the eyes of the nations—all these things in a local assembly.

But in the second epistle Paul addresses “the assembly of God which is in Corinth”. We have no knowledge of the time at which issues in Corinth were judged. We know that they were judged from the tone of the second epistle and from the facts in it. We know that a brother was, as we say, put out of fellowship. We could not nowadays say that, we would have to say he was withdrawn from, but Paul says, “Remove the wicked person from amongst yourselves”, 1 Corinthians 5: 13. A brother was put away from the local assembly. We do not know precisely at what time that was. But it seems to me that in Paul’s mind the fact that the matter was judged once attention was drawn to it—we might even say, once the Lord had Himself indicated His own point of intervention—at that point the Corinthians dealt with the matter and Paul goes on with them, “The assembly of God which is in Corinth … Grace to you, and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ”. In spite of the shameful history of Corinth Paul does not address them on any lower level than that continuous thread that he had carried in his own spirit in relation to that local assembly from the beginning of his address in the first epistle.

In Acts 18, as far as I recall, there is not exactly reference to the assembly in Corinth. Paul went there and preached the word of God—he preached in the synagogue and he preached in the house, but there is not exactly reference to the assembly. But when he wrote the epistle it was to the assembly of God in Corinth. In the second epistle, in spite of the history, Paul again addresses “the assembly of God which is in Corinth”.

I believe, beloved, that this line, this, I might even say, principle, can be traced through scripture. One only has to look at chapters 9, 10 and 11 of Romans, to see how the matter may be identified there in principle in relation to Israel. There you have a nation which has stumbled at the stumbling stone. You see them scattered, you see a people disobedient and opposing; you see a people to whom God had all the day long stretched out His hands and they had been disobedient and opposing. You see a people blinded in part until the fulness of the nations be come in; you see a people represented as branches cut out of the olive tree.
And then, what does Paul say? “So all Israel shall be saved”, Romans 11: 26. You see, he has not forfeited the principle of continuity in regard to the activities of God. What a great thing that is!

I think, beloved, that we may trace these things—we may see that if God has begun something He will see it through to the end. Failure there may be, as to which all those concerned in it would rightly be increasingly humbled, and I trust that insofar as we ourselves make any profession of anything in the present day, all the time it is coloured by increasing humility as to things with which we have been involved. But I trust, indeed I believe, that I carry the beloved brethren with me in believing that there has been continuity right through.

You might say, Where do you identify this? I could point to occasions where I can identify it, point even to the occasion which I almost describe as traumatic that occurred in 1970, when I saw beloved aged sisters weeping at what was proceeding. In that I see the thing going through. And I believe, beloved, that, in spite of our own humiliating sorrows and failure, the Lord never ceased to manifest Himself among us. I believe that that was said among us some seven years ago and I believe that the brethren remained with what was said, that the Lord did not fail.

Does this mean that the Lord condones evil? It means that the Lord comes in in order that like the Spirit of God He may raise up a banner. He would rally to Himself all who in their right judgment desire to be in the line of continuity, and eventually when the Lord acts He finds that He has enough to continue with, we may say. In His grace, as we have been reminded already, He has recovered others to it. May He in His goodness continue to recover our beloved brethren to it. I believe it is one mark of continuity in regard to what the Lord has established that there is the desire for the recovery of brethren to it. I believe that must be characteristic.

But, you may say, where then would you say that continuity ceases? I do not think that that is a difficult question to answer. I believe that continuity ceases when ground is taken different from that on which the Lord has established recovery. I believe that when there is, as was said in that historic remark, heartlessness as to the Person of Christ, then continuity is broken in upon. And until that is judged those who continue in that line are on a line that is not the continuity of what the Lord established in recovery. Many beloved brethren (we may so regard them as belonging to Christ, many having the Spirit) continue even in fellowship of that kind and we long for them, beloved. When the place of Christ is brought into challenge, then the continuity is necessarily trenched upon when it may be said, as one said at the time, that if things that were professed in the 1840’s were true, then Christ Himself needed a saviour. Does anything more need to be said to show that the line of continuity had been broken in upon there, not only by the persons who said it, but by the persons who received those who said it and by persons who received those who would receive those who said it. These things interrupt the line of continuity.
When truth is brought out as to eternal life and persons reject it and persons describe those through whom it comes as heretical, does that continue the line? Or does that interrupt it?

When persons set aside the great basis of continuity in 2 Timothy and consider that questions of unequal yokes and that kind of thing may be taken up with a measure of impunity or, at least, may be defended, is that the line of continuity? Beloved, these things depart from the line on which the Lord has indicated that things would be continued by faithful men in that epistle. And in that epistle the guideposts for us, I believe, are “the testimony of our Lord” (2 Timothy 1: 8), and “Jesus Christ raised from among the dead” (2 Timothy 2: 8), and “Let every one who names the name of the Lord withdraw from iniquity” (2 Timothy 2: 19), and “thou hast been thoroughly acquainted with my teaching” (2 Timothy 3: 10). That is the line which is given to Timothy in order that the continuity of things may be established.

Therefore, if we look to see whether there has been continuity or interruption, let us examine whether there has been a continuance in the things with which the Lord first began recovery, as I say, about one hundred and fifty years ago. If we can identify that even in feebleness there has been the intention to maintain these things or that there has been recovery to the maintenance of these things, then we may speak of continuity. If there has been departure from these things unjudged, then we would have sorrowfully to say that continuity has been broken.

Beloved brethren, what do we believe? What do we believe here tonight? Are we here in the light of the fact that humbly, even weakly, we seek to continue what the Lord first established, I say, seek to continue what the Lord first established, or have we come to it that at some point the Lord had to begin again? I do not believe so. I believe that when the suggestion was raised in this city five years ago that for one Lord’s day we should not break bread, in rejecting that, the saints were manifesting that continuity was what was in their minds in whatever humility and weakness. Beloved brethren, may the Lord confirm us in it and may He enable us in grace to defend it against any, whether from within or without, who would call the matter into question. Let not the saints be troubled by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter.
Impressions of a reading with W. Dickson
Proverbs 31: 10–31

The woman of worth is a very full type of the assembly. Her many activities are an epitome of the instruction in the book of Proverbs, the teaching finding a substantial answer in her so that she reflects her husband, as the assembly reflects Christ. There were two great lights,

“the great light to rule the day, and the small light to rule the night”, Genesis 1: 16. The Lord is absent and the assembly is to reflect Him. We should see the positive and constructive character of this woman’s activities. The passage is full of assembly characteristics in relation to, (i) cultivation and growth for the enhancement of the service of God (Proverbs 31: 16) and (ii) testimony among men (Proverbs 31: 23). There is constant reference to her hands. “Of the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard”; “She putteth her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. She stretcheth out her hand to the afflicted, and she reacheth forth her hands to the needy”. In these days, when there is so much to be done, are our activities together of this character?

In the gospels there are frequent references to the Lord Jesus using His hands. Those hands were always used for blessing, and to impart help and healing where it was needed. What we contemplate in Christ is to become formative in the saints, resulting in diligent care in relation to

His interests. Thus we are to be a means of blessing, like the sons of Levi, who were to bless in the name of Jehovah (Deuteronomy 10: 8). Paul, too, laboured. He was not reluctant to use his hands to gather sticks and lay them on the fire (Acts 28: 3). Then the viper appeared, hanging on his hand. The enemy seeks to destroy hands used in blessing. All this involves service, in which the levitical spirit should mark us. The service of the woman of worth flows out of committal to the interests of her husband, and her affection for him—“She doeth him good … all the days of her life”. Her heart’s desire is to fill out what has been entrusted to her. So the woman of worth is to find expression in each locality. No vessel is entrusted with so much as the assembly.

The first activity of this woman is that “She seeketh wool and flax”. The wool suggests the teaching of John’s epistles, leading up to love amongst ourselves. You generate the warmth of love. The flax would relate to righteousness and the teaching of Romans, leading up to the reference to the one body in Christ (Romans 12: 5). The wool and flax might not be in abundant supply—it was not abundant at Corinth, hence it had to be sought. “She putteth her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle”, showing the diligence with which she works with the materials she has acquired. There is the thought here of matters being worked out to completion. So “she maketh body linen and selleth it, and delivereth girdles unto the merchant”—giving an impression of priestly clothing, the saints being clothed suitably for the service of God and for testimony. We are so set up in grace that we can supply that which will clothe and enrich the saints. There is a divine pattern, so we are to have a positive aim and object in what we do.

There is what relates to gift, but there is also the great matter of the acceptance of responsibility, and this can, and should, begin when we are young. We can take on the levitical spirit in prayer for the saints, beginning with our local brethren. Paul speaks of Timothy as caring “with genuine feeling how ye get on”, Philippians.2: 20. That was not a matter of gift, but of concern for the welfare of the saints. We should all desire a levitical spirit. The Levites numbered about 22,000. Those actively engaged, referring to the principle of gift, were about 8,500, but all should express the levitical spirit as responsible for the Lord’s interests.
There is divine wisdom in putting us together collectively. In 2 Corinthians 1: 19 and in 1
Thessalonians 1: 1 we have Paul and Silvanus and Timotheus mentioned together. It is so important that we learn to work together, having the same affections, outlook, and objective.

You look at the pattern and labour for an answer to the divine thought. In writing to the Galatians Paul links himself with “all the brethren with me” (Galatians 1: 2), giving an impression of the affections and feelings among the brethren in support of his service to Galatia. In that epistle Paul speaks of himself as a mother, again travailing in birth for the saints, whilst in 1 Thessalonians 2, Silvanus and Timotheus thus being linked with him, Paul says, ‘ We … have been gentle in the midst of you, as a nurse would cherish her own children’

(1 Thessalonians 2: 7) and then adds, ‘ye know how, as a father his own children, we used to exhort each one of you’ (verse 11), showing that those three men were united in maternal and fatherly affections and feelings in their service to the saints. All this shows the value of coordinated work in the assembly.

Another feature in the woman of worth is that “she bringeth her food from afar”. She is global, universal, in her outlook, not parochial. Localities should not be self-contained but the truth of the one body is to govern us. That truth has been attacked in many divisions. So we have the advantage of ministry given in many parts, and all is to be valued, labour entering into its being made available to us.

It says, “She considereth a field”, that is, she considers its potentialities and would work in relation to them. Then “She perceiveth that her earning is good”; she is conscious of blessing and prosperity. As we are thus conscious of confirmation and blessing, the earning being good, there will be that which we can make available to the saints for their profit.

The assembly is the place of administration of divine blessing. A prime feature would be the gospel flowing out. The ministry meeting is another aspect of administration—what the saints may need in the way of prophetic speaking. A young brother may have an impression as to a word. Let him get to the Lord as to it, as to how it relates to what is being wrought out by Him among the saints. One should have an objective in relation to the brethren in service to them. The intent, purport, and aim of the word should be weighed up. “Her husband is known in the gates”, that is, Christ is to be expressed in all that is done.

We need to lay hold more definitely of the way the Lord manifests Himself to us at the Supper so that it may be developed and expanded among us. You would be concerned to have the substance and the spirit of what has been imparted, and to enquire as to the Lord’s mind in giving such an impression and how it can be most effectively used.

Strength and dignity are her clothing (Proverbs 31: 25). The care meeting is to be held in its own dignity as an occasion in which the interests of the Lord are faithfully cared for. Mr. Taylor stressed the dignity of the assembly and the necessity of maintaining it in the reading ‘Let not the Assembly be Charged’ (N.S. Vol. 59, p.233). The administration of the bounty of the saints is a very dignified matter.

Then it is said that “She surveyeth the ways of her household”. This is a sobering consideration relating to the fellowship. Matters should come under constant scrutiny. The woman of worth would let nothing pass, and no one would be missed out in her prayers. It is not only that there is an administration of blessing and supply, care and food, but there is also control and regulation. We have to survey matters in our localities. There may be something which requires attention. Burdens are not decreasing. The more there are in fellowship, the greater the responsibility. Something may have come in which requires attention. But let us not forget Matthew 18. Firstly, “Go, reprove him between thee and him alone” (Matthew 18: 15). That is not giving a word in the ministry meeting directed to a particular person; you serve in the way Matthew 18 indicates with a view to securing the person for the assembly.

Where these activities are proceeding, where the household is normal, what we have in verse 28 will be true, “Her children rise up and call her blessed”. Then there is the Lord’s appreciation of such diligence, ‘Many daughters have done worthily, but thou excellest them all’.
Thinking of God and looking on His ways,
As shown to me by Jesus, His own Son,
My soul has been not only moved to praise
That I should know the ways of such a One,
But moved to love, considering the heart
(Moved by desire that when these ways were done
I as myself a son should form a part
In His eternal presence, being too
Integral in Christ’s glorious counterpart—
The splendid bride joined to the Bridegroom who
Gave all for her) which from profound affection
Conceived and used these ways to carry through
Those whom He loved into complete perfection,
Washed from their sins, cleared from the power of sin, Knowing His love in Christ, the Resurrection,
And in the arms of God who drew them in
To His own countenance. No other mind
Could, pulsing to its grandest heights, begin
To think of such a plan as this, designed
By such a God; no other heart required
Such a conception for its unconfined
Expanse of love; no other love inspired
Such love as that by which God’s sons are fired.
Edinburgh
ABOVE THE STORM Flying through the tropics by night we saw, far below, a violent storm.
Vivid flashes of lightning zigzagged through great banks of cloud. But where we were all was calm and clear, the stars shining like beacons in the sky.

We all have to face storms in our lives, and how good it is that the presence of Jesus can be known in them—“About the fourth watch of the night he comes to them walking on the sea”, Mark 6: 48. What comfort there is in such an experience!—His presence in the trouble.

But there is also the fact that we can be lifted in spirit out of the area of trouble into the peace and calm of His presence. Solomon, in his prayer in 1 Kings 9, mentions all kinds of disasters and troubles and, like a refrain, he repeats his request that in all these circumstances God would hear the prayer of His people from “the heavens, the settled place of thy dwelling”. All is settled, all is peace, there. As Mr. Darby’s hymn says—
‘Our hearts resort to where Thou liv’st
In heav’n’s unclouded rays’.

HEAVENLY COLOUR Let us not be like the chameleon, changing our colour according to our surroundings. We watched one in South Africa. It was difficult at first to find him, so well did he merge with the green shoots of the tree. When coaxed on to a darker area he began to change colour to tone in with it.

A christian is to appear as a christian at school, at work—wherever he may be. Let us not change our colour to please others, or to escape the reproach of Christ. Israelites wore tassels on the corners of their garments, and a lace of blue (see Numbers 15: 38), so wherever you saw an Israelite you would know that he belonged to a nation linked with heaven. Mr. Taylor remarked as to that, ‘As we turn round the corner, maybe on the Monday after the Lord’s day, we do not lose the heavenly blue; we are not one thing on Sunday and another thing on Monday, we are heavenly on both days’ (N.S. Vol. 84 p.60).

The manger is outside what man provides for man, but God always provides for those who are content to accept whatever provision He may be pleased to make. God always has had, and always will have, a provision for those who trust in Him, and those who are in dependence on Him will prove it. It may not be luxurious, but it will always suffice for faith.
Truly dependent ones accept what is provided, and find the care of God very sweet even in outward reproach.
